facts.claim: "I Like the Way This Is Going" is written by Mark Oliver Everett (E) and credited to Eels. It is 2:35 long.
Mark Oliver Everett produced the track, and Ryan Boesch is credited as mixer on the Shazam credits.
It is track 13 of 14 on the standard Tomorrow Morning album. It sits between "That's Not Her Way" and "Mystery of Life".
Tomorrow Morning (Deluxe) came out on August 24, 2010 on E Works Records. It has 19 songs, adding a bonus EP of four non-album tracks to the 14 on the standard album.
Tomorrow Morning was recorded August–December 2009 at OneHitsville, U.S.A., in Los Feliz, California.

Credits on the deluxe edition include Koool G Murder and Ryan Boesch (programming), Wally Gagel (mixing), Dan Pinder (recording) and Dan Hersch (mastering). Robert Carranza (programming) and the Amy Davies Choir are also credited.

The lyrics are a simple love song, with the narrator listing things he likes about a partner. They include a toothy smile, hair color and watching TV together. The refrain is that he likes the way things are going.

The official Eels site calls Tomorrow Morning the brightest and most overtly uplifting work of Eels' fourteen-year career. It is the final part of a trilogy with Hombre Lobo and End Times, and Everett calls it "The redemption".
Tomorrow Morning departs from the garage rock of Hombre Lobo and the acoustic starkness of End Times. It uses electronic keyboards, drum machines, tape loops and found sounds.
Everett told Drowned in Sound that after End Times he felt there was only one direction to go, which was up. He said he did not want to go any further down.

research.lineage: Eels is Mark Oliver Everett's project, mixing off-kilter pop influences with deeply personal lyrics. This song sits in the electronic, keyboard-based uplift of the closing album of his Hombre Lobo / End Times / Tomorrow Morning trilogy.

draft:
Most love songs promise forever. **I Like The Way This Is Going** won't go that far. Eels hang the whole song on a phrase about direction, not arrival, and that small hedge is where the feeling lives. The narrator doesn't swear devotion. The narrator notices that things are trending well and says so, again and again, like someone afraid to jinx it.

The verses are a list, and the list is plain on purpose: a toothy smile, the color of someone's hair, the way their pants fit, how they stand and how they sit. Nothing grand. The best stretch is the most domestic one, watching TV together and then going to bed, so that you can "Get up and do it all again." That line carries the song's quiet thrill. Repetition, which sinks so many relationships, is the reward here. Even the weather hedges in "whichever way the wind is blowing," as if the narrator knows conditions change and is choosing to be glad anyway.

Then the past shows up, briefly. The narrator says they don't care about it, and adds that "None of it was made to last." It's a shrug, but it costs something. You don't wave off old wreckage that casually unless there was wreckage. The contentment and the old damage sit in the same verse, and the song never asks which one is truer. The answer it lands on is to look at "who you're knowing," the person in the room right now.

That fits where the song sits. Mark Oliver Everett wrote and produced it for *Tomorrow Morning*, recorded in 2009 at OneHitsville, U.S.A., in Los Feliz. The album is the last of a trilogy after *Hombre Lobo* and *End Times*. Everett called it "The redemption," and he said that after *End Times* he didn't want to go any further down. The only way left was up. This song is what up sounds like when it's still a little wary.

The arrangement keeps things easy. Acoustic guitar strums at a relaxed, moderate pace. A walking bass line strolls underneath, brushed drums give it a slight swing, and a clean electric guitar threads a melody around the vocal. The voice is slightly raspy and conversational, sung as if across a couch rather than from a stage. The sound is clean, polished and uncluttered, with room for every part to be heard. The album's mixer credit goes to Ryan Boesch. On a record that reaches for drum machines and tape loops, this one leans on older, warmer tools, and they suit a song about small comforts.

It runs short and never pushes, and that restraint is the point: it lets you feel how hopeful it is to say "so far, so good" out loud after a long time of not being able to.
